name: Lindsey Graham
role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (2003-2026); U.S. Representative (1995-2003)
summary: A conservative Republican and prominent defense and foreign-policy hawk who backed the Iraq war, NATO, Ukraine and Israel and urged force against Iran. He opposed the Affordable Care Act, sponsored federal abortion limits and favored tax cuts and balanced-budget rules, while occasionally working with Democrats on immigration reform. He became a close ally of Donald Trump after criticizing him in 2016.

notes:
Not living: died 11 July 2026 (s1, s4). Only directly documented positions are answered; no inferences beyond the low-confidence items. Views shifted over time: supported comprehensive immigration reform in 2006-2013 and stronger border enforcement later; criticized Trump in 2016 and became an ally from 2017.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 22 answers taken from it, 18 agreed, 2 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent third-model audit; full blank list and all active statements reviewed. Prior notes and sources were read, but no previous answers. The ten prioritized items yield consent-of-governed, ethnic-nation, democracy-best and elective-rulers. Natural rulers, monarchy, national rebirth, hereditary-title abolition and the small armed vanguard theory remain null: support for Pahlavi does not itself endorse monarchy, and mass uprisings are not foco theory. The single historical inference is explicitly labelled and low confidence. Election consent is contested because two witnesses describe the Georgia call differently from Graham; the allegation is not treated as judicially established. Constitutional checks are mixed in light of his expansive war-power position rather than automatically generalized from January 6. His bipartisan compromise rhetoric does not erase conservative commitments or imply that left and right are obsolete. New primary research includes lengthy foreign-policy interviews, Senate speeches, campaign captions, an encryption bill and minimum-wage hearing. His final-year programme is distinguished from later memorials: Durbin’s account is secondhand and medium confidence. The religious-school curriculum question remains null; support for public prayer is not religious instruction. Ordinary public faith and a prohibition on religious establishment are distinct. No view is inferred simply from Baptist identity. His support for modest wage adjustments does not cancel opposition to the substantial $15 proposal. Aid framed as a national-security instrument is not an asserted worldwide duty to give substantial aid. Fossil expansion and nuclear support coexist with qualified emissions reduction. Later explicit positions take precedence over earlier rhetoric. No score is derived from animal-welfare ratings or from the views of other AI-hearing participants. Nonconsensual deepfake liability does not establish a position on all pornography or on automating government. General all-drug legalization, broad AI optimism, human enhancement and the more specialized economic doctrines remain unknown. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by kind; answers that rested only on Wikipedia or OnTheIssues are re-sourced to his Voteview roll calls (House 1995-2002, Senate 2003-2026) or nulled with review history. The earlier claim that he voted against New START is not in Voteview: his two recorded New START votes (21 Dec 2010) were on amendments. His Congressional Record statements (crec: Social Security accounts, China currency, birthright, charity, traditional family, sex education, Greenland, stimulus, Armenian) were searched; those on territorial expansion, birthright citizenship, traditional family, sex education, charity, Armenian genocide and the stimulus hold no position of his on the statement. Recognition of the Armenian genocide passed the Senate by unanimous consent in 2019, with no roll call, and his 1996 House vote against an amendment tying Turkey's aid to acknowledging it is not clear evidence, so recognise-genocide is nulled.
